newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chinese, Indian leaders visit Russia.
newsitem.headline: Chinese, Indian leaders visit Russia.

text.p: Russia, upset by a rift with the West over NATO's enlargement and seeking new strategic partners in the post-Cold War world, looks east this week when it hosts leaders from China and India.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda arrived in Russia late on Monday to discuss bilateral economic relations and his visit is expected to have military cooperation high on the agenda.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen landed hours later to prepare for a visit next month by President Ziang Zemin.
Both are expected to meet President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. Qian was also due to hold talks with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

The two Asian leaders are visiting Moscow days after Yeltsin's Helsinki summit with U S. President Bill Clinton, at which they "agreed to disagree" over NATO's plans to invite former Soviet bloc states to join the Western defence alliance.

Russian officials say NATO's commitment to expansion, despite Moscow's objections, marks the end of the honeymoon period between Russia and the West which followed the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Russia is now looking for allies elsewhere. China and India, which also have strains in relations with the West, are among the most highly prized partners.
Beijing and Moscow formed a strong alliance in the early 1950s which later degenerated into bitter rivalry for leadership of the world communist movement and led to border clashes in the late 1960s.
Relations have improved dramatically since a visit to Beijing by Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev in 1989.
Russia and China say they are keen to develop a strategic partnership in the 21st century, but both countries rule out the renewal of any military or political bloc.

During his visit to Russia in late April, Jiang is expected to sign a treaty with Russia and the ex-Soviet republics of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, concluding a long-awaited accord on troop reductions along their border with China.
No details of the treaty have been revealed.
Russia's other aim is to mirror progress on the political front with rapid growth of trade and economic cooperation which could open doors wider to the huge Chinese market.
Moscow is also keen to resume its once close relations with India, especially strong in the 1960s and 1970s when New Delhi was involved in conflicts with China and U.S. ally Pakistan.

The weakness of post-Soviet Russia made special relations with it less attractive for India. This became clear in 1993 when Moscow postponed, under U.S. pressure, a $300 million contract on the sale of rocket boosters to India.
But bilateral links have started improving lately as Russia began focusing more on relations with traditional partners to its south and east.
The Russian space agency Glavkosmos said on Monday that Moscow would start supplying rocket boosters to India later this year, Itar-Tass news agency said.
Russian officials have said arms sales will be high on the agenda of Deve Gowda's visit.

Interfax news agency quoted Oleg Sidorenko, deputy head of arms trader Rosvooruzheniye, as saying the two countries were planning to launch a new long-term programme of military cooperation in the year 2000.

Detailed figures of the Russian-Indian arms trade are not officially published. But military officials have said that last year's $1.8 billion contract to sell India 40 modern SU-30MK jet fighters was the biggest between them so far.
Russia officially sells arms to 51 countries, but military officials say about 60 percent of sales go to India or China.
